questions.subtopic: Case Study 2: Technology and the 19th-Century World Economy
questions.question: Case Study 2 (Q14-Q16): The transformation of the nineteenth-century world economy was made possible by major technological innovations.\n\nQ14: Which technological innovations were crucial in linking distant agricultural hinterlands to global consumer markets?
options: Railways, steamships, and the telegraph
Aeroplanes and radar systems
Automobiles and satellite navigation
Nuclear power generators
questions.explanation: Railways brought agricultural produce from deep continental interiors to ocean ports, steamships lowered ocean transport times and costs, and the telegraph provided real-time market data across continents.

questions.subtopic: Case Study 2: Technology and the 19th-Century World Economy
questions.question: Case Study 2 (Continued): Before the advent of refrigerated shipping technology in the late 1870s:\n\nQ15: What was the primary limitation of transatlantic live cattle transport from America to Europe?
options: Live animals were eaten by sharks during sea storms
European port authorities banned all American animals due to religious taboos
Cattle refused to board steam-powered ships
High freight costs due to the enormous ship space occupied by live cattle, alongside heavy mortality and loss of weight during the voyage
questions.explanation: Live cattle took up immense ship room; many fell sick, died, or lost weight in transit, making live animal shipment inefficient and meat an expensive luxury.

questions.subtopic: Case Study 2: Technology and the 19th-Century World Economy
questions.question: Case Study 2 (Continued): How did the refrigerated cargo ship change meat consumption patterns in Britain?
options: People stopped eating meat and became vegetarians
Meat was reserved exclusively for the royal military navy
Meat prices dropped drastically, allowing the working class to add meat, butter, and eggs to their daily diet of bread and potatoes
Import of foreign meat was banned to protect domestic British cattle
questions.explanation: Refrigeration lowered the price of imported meat, transforming it from a luxury for the rich into a regular dietary item for ordinary working-class European families.

questions.subtopic: Case Study 3: Colonialism and Rinderpest in Africa
questions.question: Case Study 3 (Q17-Q18): In Africa in the 1890s, a rapid spread of cattle plague (Rinderpest) transformed the lives of people and their relations with the rest of the world.\n\nQ17: Why had European colonizers initially faced great difficulty in recruiting African labourers for their mines and plantations?
options: Africans were physically incapable of working in tropical heat
European wages were paid in cowrie shells which were illegal in Africa
African chiefs had established trade unions with European governments
Africans possessed ample land and cattle to support their own families and saw no reason to work for European wages
questions.explanation: In 19th-century Africa, land and livestock were abundant relative to the population. Pastoral and agrarian self-sufficiency meant Africans had no desire to surrender their freedom for wages.

questions.subtopic: Case Study 3: Colonialism and Rinderpest in Africa
questions.question: Case Study 3 (Continued): When rinderpest wiped out 90% of African cattle in the 1890s:\n\nQ18: How did colonial employers and governments exploit the disaster to consolidate their imperial grip?
options: They monopolized the remaining cattle resources, forcing destitute Africans to submit to mine and plantation wage labour
They vaccinated all surviving cattle for free and redistributed them to poor farmers
They abandoned all colonial territories in Africa and returned to Europe
They invited Indian indentured labourers to replace the entire African workforce
questions.explanation: Planters, mine owners, and colonial governments seized the few remaining cattle, monopolizing what was left of livestock resources and effectively forcing surviving Africans into subservient wage employment.

questions.subtopic: Case Study 4: Indian Trade and the Imperial Economy
questions.question: Case Study 4 (Q19-Q20): Over the nineteenth century, British manufacturers flooded the Indian market, while India's export profile underwent dramatic structural change.\n\nQ19: What primary goods did colonial India export to Britain and the rest of the world to replace manufactured cotton cloth?
options: Steam engines, railway carriages, and machine tools
Automobiles, chemicals, and pharmaceuticals
Raw cotton, opium, food grains, and indigo
Fine porcelain, glass, and paper
questions.explanation: India was deindustrialized and transformed into an exporter of agricultural raw materials (raw cotton, jute, indigo) and food grains to feed British factories and urban workers, along with opium for the China trade.

questions.subtopic: Case Study 4: Indian Trade and the Imperial Economy
questions.question: Case Study 4 (Continued): While Britain ran trade deficits with rapidly industrializing nations like the United States and Germany:\n\nQ20: Why was India called the 'linchpin' of Britain's nineteenth-century imperial trading balance?
options: India purchased all the surplus coal produced in Scottish mines
Britain's massive trade surplus with India was used to balance its deficits with other countries in the global multilateral settlement system
India owned 50% shares in the Bank of England
India was Britain's only trading partner in the entire world
questions.explanation: Because Britain consistently sold more to India than it bought from India, the resulting trade surplus with India was crucial in settling Britain's trade deficits with other industrialized nations worldwide.
